longo.nar: Seventy nine ninety nine. And ninety eight dollars eighty nine. The first is the most controversial price in gaming. The second is why the controversy has the maths backwards.
The first number is official. GTA Six, standard edition, seventy nine ninety nine. Launching November the nineteenth, digital only, pre-orders open since June.
The second number is what a sixty dollar game from two thousand and five costs in today's money. Ninety eight dollars and eighty nine cents.
Put them side by side and the outrage inverts. The most expensive blockbuster ever made is still cheaper, in real money, than a mid two-thousands disc.

longo.preco: from why so dear to why so cheap
longo.nar: So the honest question is not why games got so expensive. It is how they stayed this cheap — and who has been quietly paying the difference.
This video does the maths the comment section skips. No outrage, no defence of publishers. Just where the money actually went.
Five stops. The twenty year price freeze. Where the rise went into hiding. What the freeze did to the people making games. The only number that matters to a player. And a sheet you fill in yourself.
One warning before we start: every number here has an owner and a date. Official announcements, and inflation maths on public price records.
Start with the freezer. Because the strangest thing about game prices is not that they finally moved. It is how long they refused to:
From the mid two-thousands to twenty twenty, a full priced console game cost fifty nine ninety nine. Consoles changed twice. The sticker did not move once.
Meanwhile everything else in your life rose. Rent rose. Food rose. Cinema tickets and streaming rose. The game on the shelf sat still.
And a frozen sticker is not a frozen price. Inflation ate roughly forty percent of its value while it sat there.
In real terms, every year of the freeze made games cheaper. Silently, automatically, without a single press release.
Go back further and it gets starker. A Super Nintendo cartridge in the early nineties cost, in today's money, nearly double a current release.
Why would an industry freeze its own price? Because the sticker was a weapon. Two console makers anchoring at fifty nine ninety nine, each afraid to blink first.
And look closely at the twenty twenty move. Ten dollars, after fifteen years in which inflation had taken forty percent. The rise itself undershot the freeze.
The first sticker move in fifteen years came in twenty twenty: seventy dollars for the new console generation.
The second is happening now. Eighty dollars, with GTA Six as the battering ram. Two moves in twenty years.
And even after both moves, the sticker sits below where inflation alone would have carried it. That gap is the whole story.
Because that gap did not stay unpaid. Somebody built a second floor on top of the sticker, and that is our next stop.
If the front door price could not rise, the rise had to come in through the back. Here is the back door:
Here is the real headline. The price of games did not rise. It moved — out of the sticker and into everything around it.
The second floor has four rooms. Deluxe and ultimate editions. Season passes. Battle passes. And virtual currency sold in bundles that never quite match the shop prices.
Exhibit one is on the GTA Six pre-order page itself. Standard, seventy nine ninety nine. Ultimate, ninety nine ninety nine. The eighty dollar game comes with a hundred dollar option attached.
Add the passes and the add-ons, and the cost of the complete experience of a big game has roughly doubled compared to the disc era.
Which explains why both sides of the argument feel right. The sticker really is historically cheap. And your total spend really is higher than ever.
The trick has a boring name: unbundling. Sell the core for a frozen price, and price the rest of the experience separately, where inflation can run free.
Exhibit two is the seller itself. GTA Five sold over two hundred million copies — and its online mode still made billions AFTER the purchase, year upon year, through virtual currency.
Which reframes the eighty dollars. For a game built to live for a decade, the sticker is not the price. It is the entry ticket.
And do not forget the ground floor of this building: free to play. The most profitable games of the last decade charged nothing at the door. We counted that model on this channel before.
And above the second floor there is a third: subscriptions. A monthly fee that never appears in any argument about the price of a game, and never stops charging.

longo.kicker: None of this is a scandal
longo.nar: None of this is a hidden scandal. Every price is public. It is a structure — one designed so that no single number looks like a rise.

longo.sub: who paid on the other side
longo.nar: And structures have two ends. If the player's sticker was frozen, someone on the making side was absorbing the freeze:
On the other side of a frozen sticker sits a studio whose costs were never frozen.
We counted that side on this channel already: the three hundred million dollar blockbuster. Budgets that grew tenfold while the sticker grew thirty three percent.
That is the squeeze in one picture. Costs climbing for twenty years, revenue per copy flat for fifteen of them. Two lines crossing.
And the news you have been reading for three years — the layoffs, the studio closures, the cancelled projects — lives exactly where those lines cross.
Industry trackers have counted tens of thousands of games jobs lost across the last three years. Not one bad quarter — a structural wave.
Seen from that side, the eighty dollar sticker is not greed arriving early. It is arithmetic arriving late.
But honesty cuts both ways. The publishers crying over costs also built the second floor, and the second floor collects billions. The squeeze is real, and so is the workaround.
Which leaves the only question this channel cares about. Not what games should cost. What they cost YOU:
The only honest price of a game is not on the box. It is the price divided by the hours you actually play.
Take the eighty dollar blockbuster you play for a hundred hours. Eighty cents an hour.
A cinema ticket buys two hours. Do that division and the game is one of the cheapest hours of entertainment money can buy.
Now flip it. The thirty dollar impulse buy you drop after ninety minutes costs twenty dollars an hour. The expensive game is the one you do not play.
The same division works on the second floor. A pass you grind every week is cheap. A pass you bought in March and forgot by April is the most expensive item in your library.

longo.kicker: And timing is a price too
longo.nar: Timing is a price lever as well. The same game, six or twelve months after launch, routinely sells for a fraction of the sticker. Patience is the one discount nobody advertises.

longo.preco: is a choice, not a rule
longo.nar: So the launch price is a choice you make, not a rule you obey. Paying it is rational exactly when your hours will be highest at launch — which is true for some games and false for most.
Price tags start arguments. Libraries end them. Your play history already knows which purchases were worth it.
So let us turn your library into the sheet that answers this for your case, not for the comment section's:
Six lines. Any spreadsheet, or the notes app on your phone.
Games bought this year. Editions and passes on top. Subscriptions times twelve. Hours actually played, from your console's own stats. Cost per hour. And the line you decide to cut.
Lines one and two split your spend into sticker and second floor. Most people have never seen that split. It is usually the surprise.
Line three is the quiet one. Any subscription times twelve. It never feels like game spending, and it is often the biggest number on the sheet.
Line four needs no honesty test. Your console and your launcher already count your hours. Copy the number, do not estimate it.
Line five is one division: total spend over total hours. That is your personal price of gaming. Not the industry's. Yours.
Line six is the decision. Whatever scored worst per hour this year — a subscription, a pass, a genre — that is the line you cut before the next launch season.

longo.preco: prices move twice a year now
longo.nar: And date the sheet. The freeze is over — stickers move now, and passes reprice every season. An undated sheet goes stale in months.
Before we close, the three mistakes that ruin this comparison every single time:
Three mistakes, each one expensive in its own way.
First: comparing stickers across decades without inflation. Sixty dollars in two thousand five is not sixty dollars today. It is nearly a hundred.

longo.preco: judging the sticker, ignoring the floor
longo.nar: Second: judging the sticker and ignoring the second floor. The eighty is historically cheap. The eighty plus edition plus pass plus subscription is not.

longo.preco: paying for hours you never play
longo.nar: Third: paying for hours you never play. The most expensive game in your life is almost certainly one you barely opened.
The recap is on screen. Pause it and steal it. Argue with it in the comments — with numbers, preferably.
The thing almost nobody does is line two: splitting sticker from second floor. Do that once and every future purchase gets easier to judge.

longo.preco: argue the sticker in the abstract
longo.nar: One thing not to do: argue about the eighty dollars in the abstract. Without your hours, the sticker is just a number shouting at other numbers.
If you do one thing after this video, open your play stats and run the division on your last three purchases. That is the whole method.
It takes an evening, not a project. Six lines on one screen, and the first division fits in a coffee break.

longo.sub: count the fun, then buy it
longo.nar: If you ran the numbers, drop your cost per hour in the comments. I am collecting them for the next video.

longo.sub: count the fun, then buy it
longo.nar: And if you want this same maths on another corner of gaming — subscriptions, hardware, virtual currency — say which. Most requested goes first.

short.nar: GTA Six costs eighty dollars. And the maths behind the outrage is backwards.
A sixty dollar game from two thousand five costs ninety eight eighty nine in today's money. The freeze ate forty percent.
The real rise moved out of the sticker. Into editions, passes and subscriptions. The complete game roughly doubled.
And the only honest price is cost per hour played. Eighty dollars for a hundred hours is eighty cents an hour.
The full twenty year maths, and the sheet that prices YOUR library, is in the long video.

GTA 6 Costs $80: The 20-Year Price Freeze That Broke Gaming's Math

## DESCRICAO
$79.99. And $98.89. The first is the most controversial price in gaming — GTA 6, standard edition, launching November 19th, digital only, pre-orders open since June.
